title: Clean Firm Power and the Climate Question
lede: Deep decarbonization needs a source that runs when the wind is still and the sky is dark; firm clean power is the missing piece.
body: Wind and solar are essential and already the fastest-growing new generation in many places. But a grid built to fully decarbonize still has hours, days, and cold cloudy weeks when variable output falls short. Filling that gap with storage alone becomes difficult at the tail of the distribution. A source of clean firm power — dispatchable, weather-independent, low-carbon — narrows the hardest part of the problem.

Fusion is one candidate for that role, alongside advanced fission, geothermal, and long-duration storage. Kronos does not claim fusion is the only answer or a finished one. Both of our machines are today design and simulation studies, not built plants. The honest framing is that fusion could contribute to the firm-power tier if the physics and engineering close.
Available on demand, not only when weather permits
Sited near demand, reducing long transmission dependence
Steady output that complements variable renewables rather than competing with them

The breeder (Hyperion) and the burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) are studied as steady thermal and electric sources. Neither has demonstrated hardware net gain, and we make no such claim before first-of-a-kind operation. The value proposition is conditional on results we are still working to earn.
See also firm power versus intermittency and why firm power matters for the systems view.

title: The Clean-Planet Case
lede: A steady, low-emission energy source that uses little land and no combustion could relieve several planetary pressures at once.
body: Energy is upstream of almost everything

Food, water, shelter, health, and mobility all depend on energy. So do the emissions, land use, and pollution that stress the biosphere. Because energy sits upstream, a cleaner energy system propagates benefits downstream across many systems at once. That is the core of the clean-planet case.

The case for fusion is specific and bounded. Its fuels are abundant, it produces no carbon dioxide at the point of generation, and it needs no combustion. These are structural properties of the physics, not marketing. What remains unproven is whether the machines can be built to run reliably at useful output — which is exactly what our program is trying to establish, in the open.

No single technology heals a planet. The honest ambition is contribution: adding a firm, clean option to a portfolio that already includes renewables, storage, efficiency, and conservation.

The argument is also modest in a second way: benefit is conditional on the machines working. A design that stays on paper relieves nothing. That is why the clean-planet case, for us, is inseparable from the discipline of actually building and proving the hardware, in stages, in public, rather than resting on the elegance of the idea.
Read the aspiration that anchors this work in the healed-Earth aspiration.

title: Stewardship as an Engineering Discipline
lede: Stewardship is not a slogan; it is a set of design choices, measurements, and honest limits carried through every stage of the work.
body: It is easy to state environmental values and hard to encode them into engineering. Kronos treats stewardship as a discipline: choices about materials, siting, lifecycle, and disclosure that are made explicitly and recorded, not left implicit. A value that never changes a decision is decoration.
Material selection weighed for activation and end-of-life, not only performance
Designs frozen and versioned so environmental claims attach to a specific configuration
Predictions pre-registered so results can be checked against them
Data and methods published so outside reviewers can audit the footprint

The breeder (Hyperion) and burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) are studied as whole systems, including what happens to their materials over a lifetime. We treat decommissioning and activation as first-class design inputs, discussed in activation and materials choices and decommissioning thinking.

Stewardship also means restraint in claims. We do not assert environmental benefits that depend on machines behaving in ways we have not demonstrated. Where a number is contested or uncertain, we say so rather than round toward the flattering answer.

The test we apply to any stewardship claim is simple: did it change a decision? A material we would have chosen anyway, described afterward as an environmental choice, is decoration. A material we selected specifically because it activates less, at some cost to convenience, is stewardship. We try to keep our record on the second side of that line.
This connects directly to our environment, health, and safety practices — see the EHS connection.

title: The Healed-Earth Aspiration
lede: The long horizon that motivates this work: a biosphere given room to recover, powered by energy that does not cost the planet to produce.
body: We hold a long-horizon aspiration: a world where abundant clean energy relieves the pressures that drive habitat loss, pollution, and warming, giving ecosystems room to recover. We call it the healed-Earth aspiration to name the direction, not to promise a destination or a date.

Aspiration is not prediction. Fusion, if it works, would be one input among many — renewables, restoration, efficiency, changed practices, and time. Healing a biosphere is a civilizational project measured in generations, and no energy technology accomplishes it alone.

Many restoration tasks are energy-intensive: desalinating water for stressed regions, recycling materials instead of mining them, running carbon removal, powering dense cities without combustion. Abundant clean energy does not do these things by itself, but it removes the emissions penalty that currently makes them costly to the atmosphere.

<svg viewBox='0 0 420 160' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Pressure relieved allows recovery'><path d='M20 120 Q120 40 220 120 T420 120' fill='none' stroke='#D4AD5C' stroke-width='2.5'/><line x1='20' y1='120' x2='400' y2='120' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='30' y='140' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='12'>today</text><text x='300' y='140' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='12'>with room to recover</text><circle cx='120' cy='72' r='4' fill='#232C39'/><circle cx='320' cy='96' r='4' fill='#232C39'/></svg>

We are wary of the language of salvation that surrounds new energy technologies. An aspiration held honestly is a compass, not a promise. It tells us which problems are worth choosing and which claims we have not yet earned. The distance between the compass and the destination is exactly the work still in front of us.
We keep this page deliberately modest. The aspiration guides which problems we choose; the discipline in stewardship as engineering keeps us honest about how far we have actually come.

title: Energy and the Biosphere
lede: How a civilization gets its energy shapes the air, the land, the water, and the living systems that share the planet with it.
body: Every energy system draws on the biosphere and returns something to it: emissions to the air, heat to water and atmosphere, disturbance to land, and material demand to the crust. There is no zero-impact energy. The honest question is the shape and size of the footprint, and whether it fits within the planet's capacity to absorb it.
Air: combustion adds carbon dioxide and particulates; fusion involves no combustion
Land: extraction, siting, and transmission all occupy space
Water: cooling and processing draw on freshwater in many designs
Materials: construction and fuel cycles demand mining and refining

Fusion's structural advantages are in the air and materials channels: no combustion products, and fuels drawn from abundant sources. It is not free of land, water, or material demands, and we treat those honestly on their own pages — see land and footprint, water and fusion, and materials and the Earth.

The breeder and burner are being designed with these channels in view. Because the machines are not yet built, our footprint figures are engineering estimates tied to frozen designs, not measured plant data. We flag that distinction wherever numbers appear.
Thermodynamics also sets a ceiling worth naming: all energy use eventually becomes waste heat. See the biosphere and thermal limits.

title: Why Firm Power Matters
lede: Society runs on power that is there when needed; the last stretch of decarbonization is dominated by the hardest hours to cover.
body: The tail is the hard part

Getting a grid from dirty to mostly clean is largely about deploying renewables. Getting it from mostly clean to deeply clean is a different problem: covering the residual hours when demand is high and variable supply is low. That residual is small in energy but demanding in reliability, and it is where firm clean sources earn their place.

Hospitals, water treatment, cold-chain, heating in winter, and industrial processes cannot pause when the weather changes. A grid that cannot serve them at all hours is not decarbonized in any meaningful sense; it has just moved the problem to backup fossil plants that run at the worst moments.

<svg viewBox='0 0 440 180' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Variable supply with firm baseline'><line x1='30' y1='150' x2='420' y2='150' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='1.5'/><line x1='30' y1='20' x2='30' y2='150' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M30 120 Q90 60 150 110 T270 100 T390 120' fill='none' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='30' y='120' width='360' height='30' fill='#D4AD5C' opacity='0.5'/><text x='40' y='140' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='11'>firm clean floor</text><text x='250' y='70' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='11'>variable output</text></svg>

Firm clean power raises the floor so that variable sources can do the rest without fossil backup. Fusion is studied as one way to supply that floor, alongside geothermal, advanced fission, and long-duration storage. We do not claim it is proven — see clean firm power and the climate question.

Firm capacity is also what keeps a decarbonizing grid from quietly leaning on fossil peaker plants during the worst hours. Those plants run precisely when demand is highest and renewables are lowest, so a small number of stressed hours can carry an outsized share of a grid's total emissions. Raising the clean floor is how that hidden dependence is removed.
The burner housings target two demanding firm loads directly: data centers (MetroVolt) and fixed defense installations (Aegis).

title: Fusion and the Carbon Question
lede: Fusion produces no carbon dioxide at the point of generation; the honest accounting extends to construction and fuel-cycle emissions.
body: A fusion reaction fuses light nuclei; it does not burn carbon. There is no carbon dioxide, no methane, and no particulate exhaust from the reaction itself. That is a structural property of the physics, true for both the breeder (Hyperion) D-T reaction and the burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) D-3He reaction.
But lifecycle carbon is not zero

Honest carbon accounting looks beyond the point of generation. Building a plant uses steel, concrete, superconductors, and specialized materials, all of which carry embodied emissions from today's industrial supply chains. Operating and eventually decommissioning a plant also has a footprint. A credible clean-energy claim must include these, not hide behind the clean reaction.
Generation-point CO2: none, for both machines
Embodied CO2: real, from construction and materials — shared with all large infrastructure
Fuel-cycle CO2: small, tied to processing and enrichment energy sources

We treat these on lifecycle thinking and honest environmental accounting. As the grid that supplies construction energy itself decarbonizes, embodied emissions of new clean plants fall — a virtuous coupling, but not something to claim as already achieved.
We make no operating-emissions comparison from real plant data, because neither machine is built. The claim we stand behind is narrow and physical: the reaction emits no carbon dioxide.

title: Land and Footprint
lede: Energy density lets a power source do more on less land; we treat siting footprint as a design property, stated without inflation.
body: Land is finite and contested. An energy source that delivers steady power from a compact site leaves more land for habitat, agriculture, and communities. High energy density is one of fusion's structural attractions: the fuel carries enormous energy per unit mass, so the fuel-handling footprint is small.
The full footprint is more than the fuel

A fair land accounting includes the plant site, its safety and support areas, transmission to load, and the upstream mining and refining that supply construction materials. It is not only the reactor building. Because siting a plant near demand reduces transmission needs, the burner housings — MetroVolt and Aegis — are studied as co-located firm sources, which can lower the transmission share of the footprint.

<svg viewBox='0 0 420 150' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Compact site plus upstream footprint'><rect x='30' y='60' width='60' height='50' fill='#232C39'/><text x='60' y='130' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='11' text-anchor='middle'>plant site</text><rect x='120' y='75' width='90' height='35' fill='none' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='165' y='130' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='11' text-anchor='middle'>support</text><rect x='240' y='50' width='150' height='60' fill='none' stroke='#D4AD5C' stroke-width='2'/><text x='315' y='130' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='11' text-anchor='middle'>upstream mining</text></svg>

We do not publish a headline acres-per-megawatt figure, because the machines are not built and such figures are easy to game by choosing boundaries. What we commit to is drawing the boundary honestly when we do report footprint, per honest environmental accounting.

A further honesty is that density is a claim about the fuel and the reactor, not automatically about the whole enterprise. We commit to counting the site, its support and safety areas, the path to load, and the upstream supply chain, so that a compact core is never mistaken for a compact footprint overall.
Land also intersects biodiversity: less disturbed ground means more intact habitat. See energy and the biosphere.

title: Water and Fusion
lede: Thermal power plants use water for cooling; we treat water draw as a real constraint and a design choice, not an afterthought.
body: Most thermal power plants — fossil, fission, and thermal fusion alike — reject heat to the environment, and many do so using water. In water-stressed regions this is a genuine environmental constraint. Any honest clean-energy program has to name its water demand rather than assume it away.
Cooling method: once-through, wet-tower, dry, or hybrid — each trades water for efficiency and land
Siting: coastal and industrial sites change what water is available and at what ecological cost
The burner's direct energy conversion converts part of the output without a full thermal cycle, which can reduce the heat that must be rejected

The burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) uses D-3He with a direct-energy-conversion stage, so a portion of its output bypasses the steam cycle. That structurally reduces the thermal load compared with a purely thermal machine of the same output, though it does not eliminate cooling needs. The breeder (Hyperion) is a thermal machine and would follow conventional thermal-plant water practice.

<svg viewBox='0 0 420 150' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Direct conversion reduces heat rejected'><rect x='30' y='40' width='100' height='60' rx='6' fill='#232C39'/><text x='80' y='75' fill='#D4AD5C' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle'>plasma</text><line x1='130' y1='60' x2='210' y2='60' stroke='#D4AD5C' stroke-width='2'/><text x='170' y='52' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='10' text-anchor='middle'>direct</text><line x1='130' y1='90' x2='210' y2='90' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='2'/><text x='170' y='110' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='10' text-anchor='middle'>thermal</text><rect x='210' y='70' width='90' height='40' fill='none' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='255' y='95' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='11' text-anchor='middle'>cooling</text></svg>
We report no plant water figures, because no plant exists. The commitment here is to treat water as a first-class constraint in siting and design — part of stewardship as engineering.

title: Materials and the Earth
lede: Every machine is drawn from the crust; responsible design weighs what it takes to build, run, and eventually retire the hardware.
body: Superconducting magnets, structural steel, shielding, and specialized alloys all begin as mined ore. A clean-energy machine is not clean if we ignore what it costs the Earth to construct. Kronos treats material demand as part of the environmental ledger, alongside emissions and land.
Quantity: compact, high-field designs aim to do more with less structural mass
Recyclability: favoring materials that can re-enter supply chains at end of life
Activation: choosing materials that become less problematic when exposed to neutrons
Supply resilience: avoiding dependence on the most constrained materials where alternatives exist

The breeder's high peak field of 16.84 T and the burner's 26.49 T plug are demanding on magnet materials, including rare-earth barium copper oxide (REBCO) superconductors. We are open that these are material-intensive components and study their sourcing and end-of-life explicitly, rather than treating magnets as an environmental free lunch.
Neutron exposure changes materials over time — see activation and materials choices. Planning for retirement from the start is covered in decommissioning thinking.

We are candid that a compact, high-field machine is materially demanding in a different way than a large, low-field one: it asks less total mass but more from specialized components. The environmental ledger is therefore a trade, not a free win, and we treat it as one to be optimized openly rather than a headline to be claimed.
The larger shift we work toward is described in from extraction to stewardship: using abundant energy to recycle rather than perpetually mine.

title: Fusion Fuel and Abundance
lede: Fusion draws on some of the most abundant materials available; abundance reduces the geopolitical and extractive pressure of fuel supply.
body: The breeder (Hyperion) runs on deuterium and tritium. Deuterium is a stable hydrogen isotope present in ordinary water; tritium is bred in-machine from lithium. The breeder is designed to make its own tritium, with a tritium breeding ratio studied as a design lever across values of 1.1, 1.5, and 1.8. The burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) runs on deuterium and helium-3.
Why abundance is an environmental property

Scarce fuels drive extraction into ever more marginal and damaging deposits, and concentrate supply in few hands. Abundant fuels relieve both pressures. Deuterium is effectively inexhaustible on human timescales, and lithium, while finite, is widely distributed. This does not make the fuel cycle impact-free, but it changes its character.

<svg viewBox='0 0 420 150' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Deuterium from water, tritium bred from lithium'><circle cx='70' cy='75' r='30' fill='none' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='2'/><text x='70' y='80' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='11' text-anchor='middle'>water</text><line x1='100' y1='75' x2='150' y2='75' stroke='#D4AD5C' stroke-width='2'/><text x='125' y='65' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='10' text-anchor='middle'>D</text><rect x='150' y='55' width='90' height='40' rx='6' fill='#232C39'/><text x='195' y='80' fill='#D4AD5C' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='11' text-anchor='middle'>breeder</text><circle cx='340' cy='75' r='30' fill='none' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='2'/><text x='340' y='80' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='10' text-anchor='middle'>lithium</text><line x1='310' y1='75' x2='240' y2='75' stroke='#D4AD5C' stroke-width='2'/><text x='275' y='65' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='10' text-anchor='middle'>T bred</text></svg>

Helium-3 for the burner is genuinely scarce on Earth. We are candid that a large burner fleet would depend on a helium-3 supply that does not yet exist at scale. That is a real gate on the burner path, discussed in helium-3 and the planet, not something we paper over.

Abundance also changes the politics of energy. Fuels concentrated in a few deposits invite competition and coercion over their supply; fuels drawn from ordinary water and widely distributed lithium are harder to weaponize. That is an environmental benefit in the broad sense, because conflict over resources is itself a driver of ecological harm.
See the tritium cycle and the planet for how breeding closes the fuel loop.

title: Fusion Waste, Stated Honestly
lede: Fusion produces no long-lived high-level fuel waste, but neutron activation of structures is real; we describe both plainly.
body: What fusion does and does not produce

Fusion does not produce the long-lived, high-level spent fuel associated with fission. There is no chain reaction to run away and no actinide waste stream from the fuel. That is a genuine and important difference. But fusion is not waste-free, and saying so would be dishonest.

The breeder (Hyperion) is a D-T machine, and D-T fusion releases 14 MeV neutrons. Those neutrons activate the surrounding structure over time, making some components radioactive. The relevant waste is therefore activated structural material, not spent fuel. Its hazard is generally shorter-lived than fission high-level waste and depends strongly on which materials are chosen.
Activated structures: real, material-dependent, generally shorter-lived hazard
The burner has a much lower neutron fraction (5.44%), reducing activation relative to a D-T machine of similar output

Because the burner's D-3He reaction is largely aneutronic, only 5.44% of its energy appears as neutrons. This materially reduces its activation burden compared with the breeder — a structural advantage we can state, though the burner depends on scarce helium-3 as noted in helium-3 and the planet.
Choosing low-activation materials is an active design lever — see activation and materials choices and radiological honesty.

title: Air Quality and the End of Combustion
lede: Combustion harms health long before it changes the climate; a source that does not burn anything removes that local burden entirely.
body: The near-term human cost of burning

Long before carbon dioxide warms the planet, combustion products harm people who breathe them. Fine particulates, nitrogen oxides, sulfur oxides, and other pollutants from burning fossil fuels and biomass are linked to respiratory and cardiovascular harm. This is a present, local cost paid disproportionately by communities near power plants and busy roads.

Neither the breeder (Hyperion) nor the burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) burns fuel. The reactions fuse light nuclei; there is no flue gas, no particulate exhaust, and no products of combustion to release into the air. For local air quality, a non-combustion firm source is categorically different from a fossil plant.

<svg viewBox='0 0 420 150' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Combustion exhaust versus none'><rect x='40' y='60' width='50' height='60' fill='#232C39'/><path d='M55 60 q-8 -20 6 -30 q10 -8 4 -20' fill='none' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M75 60 q-8 -18 6 -28' fill='none' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='2'/><text x='65' y='138' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='10' text-anchor='middle'>combustion</text><rect x='250' y='60' width='50' height='60' rx='6' fill='none' stroke='#D4AD5C' stroke-width='2.5'/><text x='275' y='95' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='14' text-anchor='middle'>—</text><text x='275' y='138' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='10' text-anchor='middle'>no exhaust</text></svg>

This is one of the clearest, least contested environmental statements we can make, because it follows directly from the physics rather than from plant performance. It holds whether or not the machines ever reach economic net gain.

The health burden of combustion is not evenly distributed. Communities beside highways, ports, and power plants breathe more of it, and often have the least say in where such infrastructure is built. A firm source that emits nothing at the point of generation is therefore not only an air-quality improvement but a matter of who bears the cost of the power everyone uses.
The climate side of the same coin is covered in fusion and the carbon question.

title: The Energy-Poverty Problem
lede: Hundreds of millions live with too little reliable energy; a clean-planet vision that ignores their needs is neither just nor durable.
body: Clean and enough are both required

Environmental strategy sometimes speaks only of reducing energy use. But large parts of the world use too little energy for health, education, and dignity. A vision of a healed planet that quietly assumes everyone consumes as little as the poorest is neither just nor stable. People will and should seek more energy; the task is to make more energy clean.
Why firm clean power is relevant here

Communities building out energy for the first time need reliability as much as cleanliness. Intermittent supply without storage cannot run a clinic's cold chain or a school's evening classes. Firm clean sources — fusion among several candidates — could let regions leapfrog toward energy that is both sufficient and low-emission, rather than choosing between the two.
Enough energy is a precondition for health, education, and opportunity
Clean and firm together avoid the false choice between poverty and pollution
Compact, sited generation reduces dependence on long, fragile transmission

We hold no illusion that fusion, unbuilt, serves anyone today. This page states a value that shapes what we are building toward: energy abundance as a route out of both poverty and pollution, not a luxury for the already-rich. See building to uplift humanity.
The equity dimension continues in the moral case for clean energy.

title: Firm Power vs. Intermittency
lede: Variable and firm generation are complements, not rivals; the cleanest grids will likely use both, matched to what each does best.
body: It is tempting to frame the energy debate as renewables versus everything else. The systems view is different: variable renewables and firm clean sources solve different parts of the same problem. Renewables provide abundant energy when conditions allow; firm sources cover the residual reliably. A grid using both can be cleaner and more resilient than one leaning entirely on either.

<svg viewBox='0 0 440 170' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Variable plus firm equals reliable clean grid'><rect x='30' y='40' width='110' height='90' rx='6' fill='none' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='85' y='30' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='11' text-anchor='middle'>variable</text><path d='M40 100 Q65 60 90 100 T140 100' fill='none' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='2'/><text x='190' y='90' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='18' text-anchor='middle'>+</text><rect x='240' y='40' width='110' height='90' rx='6' fill='none' stroke='#D4AD5C' stroke-width='2'/><text x='295' y='30' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='11' text-anchor='middle'>firm</text><rect x='250' y='95' width='90' height='25' fill='#D4AD5C' opacity='0.5'/><text x='400' y='90' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='18' text-anchor='middle'>=</text></svg>

This framing keeps us honest about our own place. Kronos is not building a rival to solar; we are studying a firm clean source that could complement it. Fusion sits among candidate firm technologies — geothermal, advanced fission, long-duration storage — and must earn its role on merit, which for us means first building and proving the machines.

The complementarity is quantitative, not merely rhetorical. As a grid adds more variable generation, the value of each additional panel or turbine during already-sunny or already-windy hours falls, while the value of capacity that can cover the remaining dark, still hours rises. Firm clean sources and renewables therefore grow more useful to each other, not less, as decarbonization deepens.
See fusion among clean technologies for why we reject either-or thinking, and why firm power matters for the reliability case.

title: Decarbonizing the Hard-to-Abate
lede: Some sectors resist electrification and variable renewables; high-temperature, dispatchable clean heat and power could reach them.
body: Much of the emissions conversation focuses on electricity and light transport, where renewables and batteries are winning. Harder to reach are heavy industry, high-temperature process heat, and continuous industrial loads that cannot tolerate interruption. These hard-to-abate sectors are a large share of remaining emissions and lack easy substitutes.
What a firm high-grade source offers
Continuous operation for processes that cannot cycle with the weather
High-grade heat for industry that electric resistance struggles to supply economically
Siting near industrial load, reducing transmission dependence

A thermal fusion source like the breeder (Hyperion) produces high-grade heat, not only electricity, which is relevant to industrial heat demand. The burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) targets continuous electric loads directly. Neither is proven, and we make no claim that fusion has abated any emissions to date; the point is which problems the technology is aimed at if it succeeds.

<svg viewBox='0 0 420 140' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Firm source serving continuous industrial load'><rect x='30' y='50' width='90' height='50' rx='6' fill='#232C39'/><text x='75' y='80' fill='#D4AD5C' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='11' text-anchor='middle'>firm source</text><line x1='120' y1='75' x2='200' y2='75' stroke='#D4AD5C' stroke-width='3'/><rect x='200' y='45' width='100' height='60' fill='none' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='250' y='80' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='11' text-anchor='middle'>industry</text></svg>

These sectors matter disproportionately because they are where emissions concentrate once electricity and light transport are addressed. A clean firm source that supplies both continuous power and high-grade heat could reach loads that batteries and variable renewables struggle to serve, though whether fusion fills that role depends entirely on the machines closing the physics first.
Data centers are a fast-growing continuous load; the burner housing MetroVolt targets them directly — see data centers and clean power.

title: Data Centers and Clean Power
lede: Computing demand is growing fast and runs continuously; the burner housing MetroVolt is studied as a co-located firm clean source.
body: Data centers run around the clock and their electricity demand is rising quickly. Powering them with fossil generation ties a growing digital economy to a growing emissions source. Powering them with variable renewables alone is hard because the load never pauses. This is a textbook case for firm clean power sited near demand.

MetroVolt is one of the two housings for the burner (Aegis / MetroVolt), the D-3He tandem-mirror generator. Its intended role is a compact, co-located firm source for data-center-scale continuous load. Co-location reduces transmission dependence, and the burner's direct energy conversion and low neutron fraction (5.44%) shape its environmental profile favorably relative to a purely thermal machine.

<svg viewBox='0 0 420 140' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Co-located generator and data center'><rect x='40' y='50' width='80' height='55' rx='6' fill='#232C39'/><text x='80' y='82' fill='#D4AD5C' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='10' text-anchor='middle'>MetroVolt</text><line x1='120' y1='77' x2='190' y2='77' stroke='#D4AD5C' stroke-width='3'/><g stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='1.5' fill='none'><rect x='200' y='50' width='20' height='55'/><rect x='230' y='50' width='20' height='55'/><rect x='260' y='50' width='20' height='55'/></g><text x='240' y='125' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='10' text-anchor='middle'>data center</text></svg>

We are careful with claims: MetroVolt is a design and simulation study. It has not been built, and we assert no operating performance. The environmental argument is conditional — if the burner closes, it could supply continuous compute load without combustion. The helium-3 dependence remains a real gate; see helium-3 and the planet.

There is a further reason siting matters for compute. Moving large amounts of power over long distances loses energy and exposes the load to grid disturbances. A firm source next to the racks it feeds shortens that path. It also means the environmental profile of the computing can be tied to a single, auditable generation source rather than an averaged grid mix.

title: Defense Installations and Clean Power
lede: Fixed installations need power that is firm, secure, and low-emission; the burner housing Aegis is studied for that role.
body: Firm power where fuel logistics are a liability

Fixed installations often depend on delivered fuel and long supply lines, which are both an emissions source and a vulnerability. A firm clean source generated on site changes that equation: continuous power without a fuel convoy and without combustion. Aegis is the burner housing studied for fixed defense installations — not naval platforms.

Aegis and MetroVolt are two housings of the same burner (Aegis / MetroVolt), the D-3He tandem-mirror generator with a 26.49 T plug and direct energy conversion. Aegis targets fixed sites where reliability and reduced logistical dependence matter. Its low neutron fraction (5.44%) and direct conversion shape a favorable environmental profile relative to a purely thermal machine of similar output.
On-site firm power reduces reliance on delivered fuel
No combustion means no local exhaust at the installation

The environmental relevance is that reducing fuel logistics reduces both emissions and disturbance associated with moving and burning fuel. As with all our claims, this is conditional on the burner closing; Aegis is a design and simulation study, not built hardware, and depends on a helium-3 supply that does not yet exist at scale — see helium-3 and the planet.

title: The Tritium Cycle and the Planet
lede: The breeder makes its own tritium from lithium; a closed fuel loop reduces external supply demand and its environmental reach.
body: Tritium is scarce in nature and radioactive with a short half-life. Rather than depend on an external tritium supply, the breeder (Hyperion) is designed to breed tritium in place from lithium using the neutrons the D-T reaction produces. A machine that makes its own fuel reduces the extraction, transport, and handling that an external supply would require.
Breeding ratio as a design lever

The tritium breeding ratio (TBR) is how much tritium the machine produces per unit consumed. Kronos studies TBR as a design lever across 1.1, 1.5, and 1.8 rather than asserting a single value. A ratio above one means the machine can sustain itself and, in principle, provision the next machine — a property with fuel-security and environmental implications.
Self-breeding reduces reliance on scarce external tritium
Lithium is the feedstock, widely distributed though finite
TBR treated honestly as a range, not a settled number

<svg viewBox='0 0 420 150' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Tritium bred from lithium inside breeder'><circle cx='210' cy='75' r='55' fill='none' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M210 20 A55 55 0 0 1 258 100' fill='none' stroke='#D4AD5C' stroke-width='3' marker-end='url(#a)'/><defs><marker id='a' markerWidth='8' markerHeight='8' refX='4' refY='4' orient='auto'><path d='M0 0 L8 4 L0 8 z' fill='#D4AD5C'/></marker></defs><text x='210' y='72' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='11' text-anchor='middle'>Li + n</text><text x='210' y='90' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='11' text-anchor='middle'>→ T</text></svg>

Handling any breeding blanket and tritium inventory demands care, and we do not minimize that. But the environmental logic of breeding is sound: a machine that manufactures its own fuel from a widely distributed feedstock avoids the mining, transport, and handling that an external tritium supply chain would otherwise impose across many sites.
Tritium handling carries real safety and environmental responsibilities, which we treat under radiological honesty. Fuel abundance more broadly is covered in fusion fuel and abundance.

title: Helium-3 and the Planet
lede: The burner's fuel is largely aneutronic and clean in reaction, but helium-3 is scarce on Earth; we name that gate plainly.
body: A cleaner reaction, a harder supply

The burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) fuses deuterium with helium-3. This reaction is largely aneutronic: only 5.44% of its energy appears as neutrons, compared with the neutron-dominated D-T reaction. Fewer neutrons means less activation of surrounding structure and a lighter waste burden. Direct energy conversion further shapes a favorable environmental profile.

Helium-3 is genuinely scarce on Earth. A large burner fleet would require a helium-3 supply that does not currently exist at scale. We do not hide this behind the clean reaction. It is a real, unresolved gate on the burner path, and any environmental benefit of the burner is conditional on that supply problem being solved.
Reaction advantage: low neutron fraction (5.44%), less activation
Conversion advantage: direct energy conversion reduces thermal load
Supply constraint: helium-3 scarcity is a genuine, unsolved gate

<svg viewBox='0 0 420 140' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Low neutron fraction of D-He3'><rect x='40' y='55' width='300' height='30' fill='none' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='1.5'/><rect x='40' y='55' width='16' height='30' fill='#D4AD5C'/><text x='48' y='105' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='10' text-anchor='middle'>5.44% n</text><text x='210' y='105' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='10' text-anchor='middle'>~95% charged particles → direct conversion</text></svg>

We keep the two facts deliberately side by side so neither hides the other. The reaction's cleanliness is a genuine physics advantage that would matter if the burner closes. The supply scarcity is a genuine obstacle that no amount of clean-reaction language dissolves. Honest communication about the burner means always presenting both, which is why this page refuses to lead with only the good half.
We treat the reaction's cleanliness as a physics fact and the supply as an open problem, side by side. Neither cancels the other. See fusion waste, stated honestly and what we will not claim.

title: Neutrons, Isotopes, and Human Health
lede: The breeder's 14 MeV neutrons can produce medical and industrial isotopes, extending the machine's benefit beyond electricity.
body: The breeder (Hyperion) produces 14 MeV neutrons as an inherent part of the D-T reaction. Beyond breeding tritium, those neutrons can produce isotopes used in medicine and industry. Some medical isotopes today depend on aging reactors and fragile supply chains; a neutron source designed for reliability could steady that supply.
Why this belongs on an environment page

Environmental stewardship and human health are not separate goals. A machine whose neutrons support diagnostics, treatment, and materials analysis delivers benefit that is not measured in megawatt-hours. It also means the breeder's value does not rest solely on grid electricity, which matters while the electricity case is still being proven.
Medical isotopes for diagnosis and treatment
Industrial isotopes for materials analysis and quality control
A more resilient supply than aging single-purpose reactors

The breeder's product set is studied as roughly 4 kg/yr of tritium-class output plus about 1.97 kg/yr of helium-3, together with the 14 MeV neutron flux. These are design-study figures tied to a frozen configuration, not measured plant output; the machine is not built.

<svg viewBox='0 0 420 130' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Neutrons branching to uses'><rect x='30' y='50' width='90' height='40' rx='6' fill='#232C39'/><text x='75' y='75' fill='#D4AD5C' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='11' text-anchor='middle'>14 MeV n</text><line x1='120' y1='60' x2='190' y2='35' stroke='#D4AD5C' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='120' y1='70' x2='190' y2='70' stroke='#D4AD5C' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='120' y1='80' x2='190' y2='105' stroke='#D4AD5C' stroke-width='2'/><text x='260' y='40' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='11'>medical isotopes</text><text x='260' y='74' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='11'>tritium breeding</text><text x='260' y='110' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='11'>materials analysis</text></svg>

Framing this honestly matters: isotope production is a demonstrated use of neutron sources generally, but the breeder itself is unbuilt, so we describe a designed capability rather than delivered doses. What the design offers is optionality — value that does not depend solely on the electricity case, and that keeps human health within view of a machine whose primary job is energy.
See the tritium cycle for how the same neutrons close the fuel loop.

title: Lifecycle Thinking
lede: A plant's footprint spans construction, operation, and retirement; we account for the whole life, not the flattering middle.
body: Cradle to grave, not cradle to switch-on

The temptation in clean-energy communication is to report only the clean operating phase and ignore the emissions and materials of building and retiring the plant. Lifecycle thinking rejects that. The honest footprint of any energy source spans mining and manufacturing, construction, operation, maintenance, and decommissioning.
Materials: mining, refining, and manufacturing of components
Construction: energy and emissions to build the plant
Operation: fuel cycle, water, and maintenance over the plant's life
End of life: decommissioning and disposal or recycling of activated material

<svg viewBox='0 0 440 120' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Lifecycle phases'><line x1='30' y1='70' x2='410' y2='70' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='2'/><g fill='#D4AD5C'><circle cx='70' cy='70' r='6'/><circle cx='170' cy='70' r='6'/><circle cx='270' cy='70' r='6'/><circle cx='370' cy='70' r='6'/></g><g fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='10' text-anchor='middle'><text x='70' y='95'>materials</text><text x='170' y='95'>build</text><text x='270' y='95'>operate</text><text x='370' y='95'>retire</text></g></svg>

For fusion, the operating phase is structurally clean — no combustion, no high-level fuel waste. The honest work is in the other phases: embodied emissions of magnets and structure, and activated material at end of life. We treat these on activation and materials and decommissioning thinking.

The discipline cuts against a common failure mode in clean-energy claims, where the clean operating phase is advertised and the dirty construction phase is omitted. By insisting on the whole life, we make it harder to flatter ourselves, and we give reviewers a complete boundary to check rather than a curated slice designed to look good.
Because the machines are design studies, our lifecycle figures are estimates tied to frozen designs. We say so, per honest environmental accounting.

title: Honest Environmental Accounting
lede: The boundary you draw determines the number you get; we set boundaries transparently and refuse to publish figures we cannot defend.
body: Almost any environmental metric can be made to look good or bad by choosing where to draw the system boundary. Count only the reaction and fusion looks pristine; count global supply chains and every technology carries a footprint. Honest accounting means stating the boundary explicitly and applying it consistently across comparisons.
State the system boundary whenever we report a footprint metric
Apply the same boundary to ourselves and to comparisons
Distinguish measured data from design-study estimates
Publish the method so others can check the number

Because neither the breeder nor the burner is built, we currently have no measured plant data. Any environmental figure we give is an engineering estimate tied to a specific frozen design, and we label it that way. We will not present an estimate as if it were an operating measurement.

This discipline mirrors our scientific practice: pre-registered predictions, published data with DOIs, and reproducible analysis. Environmental honesty is the same honesty applied to footprint. See reproducibility as environmental trust and what we will not claim.

The failure we most want to avoid is the comparison that quietly uses one boundary for our technology and a wider one for the alternative. Such comparisons are technically true and deeply misleading. Committing in advance to a single, disclosed boundary for both sides is the simplest guard against that kind of dishonesty.

<svg viewBox='0 0 420 130' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Same boundary applied consistently'><rect x='40' y='40' width='150' height='60' fill='none' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='1.5' stroke-dasharray='5 4'/><text x='115' y='75' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='11' text-anchor='middle'>our system</text><rect x='230' y='40' width='150' height='60' fill='none' stroke='#D4AD5C' stroke-width='2' stroke-dasharray='5 4'/><text x='305' y='75' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='11' text-anchor='middle'>comparison</text><text x='210' y='118' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='10' text-anchor='middle'>same boundary both sides</text></svg>

title: The Precautionary Approach
lede: Where consequences could be serious and knowledge is incomplete, we design conservatively and test before we scale.
body: The precautionary approach holds that when an action could cause serious harm and the science is incomplete, the burden is on demonstrating safety rather than on proving harm first. For an energy technology handling radioactive materials and high energy densities, this is not optional caution; it is the responsible default.
Design and simulate exhaustively before building hardware
Prove behavior at small scale before committing to fleets
Choose conservative materials and margins where uncertainty is high
Pre-register predictions so surprises are visible, not buried

Our staged timeline embodies this: breeder construction begins Q2 2027, a first-of-a-kind machine targets first tritium around 2030, and only-then-proven designs progress to next-of-a-kind and beyond. We make no hardware net-gain claim before the first-of-a-kind operates. Scaling follows demonstration, not hope.

The precautionary approach also disciplines our language. We do not describe unbuilt machines as if their environmental benefits were realized. See humility about what we don't know and designing digitally before building.

Applied poorly, precaution becomes an excuse for paralysis. We reject that reading. The point is not to avoid all action but to sequence it so that the largest, least reversible commitments come after the evidence that justifies them. Testing a first-of-a-kind machine before committing to a fleet is precaution and progress at once.
