title: Designing in the Open, for the Planet
lede: Environmental claims deserve public scrutiny; we publish papers, data, and DOIs so anyone can check our footprint reasoning.
body: A private claim of environmental benefit asks the public to trust an assertion it cannot verify. Kronos works differently. We publish our physics papers, open our data, register digital object identifiers (DOIs), and license our work openly so that outside reviewers can examine not just our performance claims but the reasoning behind our environmental ones.
What open design gives the environment
External review can catch errors before they scale into hardware
Footprint methods can be audited, not just asserted
Other teams can build on verified results rather than repeat mistakes
The public can hold specific, dated claims to account

This is the same open-science flywheel that drives our technical credibility, applied to environmental trust. Publishing a claim with its data and method is a stronger environmental commitment than any slogan, because it can be checked and, if wrong, corrected.

<svg viewBox='0 0 420 150' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Publish, data, DOI, review cycle'><circle cx='210' cy='75' r='58' fill='none' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='2'/><g font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='10' fill='#232C39' text-anchor='middle'><text x='210' y='28'>publish</text><text x='283' y='80'>open data</text><text x='210' y='130'>DOI</text><text x='135' y='80'>review</text></g><circle cx='210' cy='17' r='4' fill='#D4AD5C'/><circle cx='268' cy='75' r='4' fill='#D4AD5C'/><circle cx='210' cy='133' r='4' fill='#D4AD5C'/><circle cx='152' cy='75' r='4' fill='#D4AD5C'/></svg>

Openness carries a real cost in effort and exposure: publishing means inviting criticism and admitting error in public. We accept that cost because the alternative — asking the public to trust unverifiable environmental claims — is exactly the pattern that has eroded confidence in so many industrial promises. Verifiability is the burden and the point.
See the open-science flywheel and reproducibility as environmental trust for how this works in practice.

title: Reproducibility as Environmental Trust
lede: A result others can reproduce is one the public can trust; our reproducible analysis record extends to environmental reasoning.
body: In science, a result matters only if others can reproduce it from the same inputs. Kronos maintains a reproducible analysis record — a documented set of analyses that can be re-run to obtain the same outputs. This is the backbone of technical credibility, and it applies equally to environmental claims that rest on those analyses.
Why it matters for the planet

Environmental decisions are high-stakes and often irreversible. A footprint estimate that cannot be reproduced is an opinion. One that can be re-run, checked, and challenged is evidence. Reproducibility turns environmental communication from persuasion into verification.
Inputs, methods, and code documented so analyses can be re-run
Outputs traceable to specific frozen design configurations
Errors, once found, correctable in the open rather than hidden
The same rigor for footprint reasoning as for physics results

<svg viewBox='0 0 420 130' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Same inputs reproduce same result'><rect x='30' y='45' width='90' height='40' rx='6' fill='none' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='75' y='70' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='10' text-anchor='middle'>inputs</text><line x1='120' y1='65' x2='300' y2='65' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='1.5'/><rect x='300' y='45' width='90' height='40' rx='6' fill='none' stroke='#D4AD5C' stroke-width='2'/><text x='345' y='70' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='10' text-anchor='middle'>same result</text><text x='210' y='55' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='9' text-anchor='middle'>re-run →</text></svg>

Our reproducible record spans dozens of analyses, each documented so it can be re-run rather than merely believed. When an environmental claim rests on one of those analyses, the claim inherits that same standard: it can be checked at its source. This is what separates a footprint we can defend from a footprint we merely assert.
This record is anchored to our published papers and their DOIs — see designing in the open and honest environmental accounting.

title: The Open-Science Flywheel
lede: Publishing, sharing data, and inviting replication compound into trust and better designs — the engine behind our environmental credibility.
body: Open science is not charity; it is a flywheel. Each published result, with its data and DOI, invites replication. Replication catches errors and confirms strengths. Confirmed results attract collaboration, which produces better designs, which produce more results worth publishing. Turn after turn, credibility and quality compound.
Publish results with methods and data
Register DOIs so the work is citable and permanent
Improve the design from what is learned, then publish again

<svg viewBox='0 0 300 240' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Open science flywheel'><circle cx='150' cy='120' r='80' fill='none' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M150 40 A80 80 0 0 1 230 120' fill='none' stroke='#D4AD5C' stroke-width='3'/><path d='M226 110 l6 12 l-13 -2 z' fill='#D4AD5C'/><g font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='12' fill='#232C39' text-anchor='middle'><text x='150' y='30'>publish</text><text x='250' y='124'>replicate</text><text x='150' y='218'>improve</text><text x='50' y='124'>collaborate</text></g><g fill='#D4AD5C'><circle cx='150' cy='40' r='5'/><circle cx='230' cy='120' r='5'/><circle cx='150' cy='200' r='5'/><circle cx='70' cy='120' r='5'/></g></svg>

For the planet, this matters because environmental trust cannot be asserted; it accrues through verifiable openness. The same wheel that builds our physics credibility builds the credibility of our environmental claims. See designing in the open, for the planet.

The flywheel has inertia in both directions, which is why we guard it. A single unreproducible or overstated result slows every later turn by making replication harder and trust scarcer. Keeping each turn honest — data attached, predictions pre-registered, errors corrected in public — is what lets the wheel keep gaining speed instead of seizing.
It is also why we do not treat competitors as enemies: shared open results lift the whole field — see fusion among clean technologies.

title: Pre-Registered Predictions and Honesty
lede: We state falsifiable predictions before results arrive, so success and failure are both visible — the same honesty we owe the planet.
body: It is easy to explain any result after the fact. Pre-registration means stating a falsifiable prediction before the experiment or analysis, so that the outcome can genuinely confirm or refute it. Kronos maintains pre-registered, falsifiable predictions as a matter of scientific discipline. This makes our claims accountable rather than retrofitted.
Why this is an environmental commitment

Environmental trust is repeatedly eroded by predictions that quietly move after results disappoint. Pre-registration is the antidote: if a machine misses a target, the record shows it plainly. A program willing to be proven wrong in public is one whose environmental claims can be believed when they are right.
Predictions stated before results, with clear pass/fail criteria
Outcomes recorded against the original prediction, not a revised one
Failures kept visible, not reframed as successes

<svg viewBox='0 0 420 130' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Prediction then result compared'><rect x='30' y='45' width='120' height='40' rx='6' fill='#232C39'/><text x='90' y='70' fill='#D4AD5C' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='11' text-anchor='middle'>prediction</text><line x1='150' y1='65' x2='270' y2='65' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='1.5' stroke-dasharray='4 4'/><rect x='270' y='45' width='120' height='40' rx='6' fill='none' stroke='#D4AD5C' stroke-width='2'/><text x='330' y='70' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='11' text-anchor='middle'>result</text><text x='210' y='105' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='10' text-anchor='middle'>compared honestly</text></svg>

There is a quiet cost to this practice: pre-registration means we cannot retroactively claim we expected whatever happened. That is precisely its value. A field that only ever explains results after the fact accumulates confidence it has not earned. By fixing the target first, we let reality grade us, and we let the public watch it happen.
This connects to our staged timeline: we predict, we build, we check. No hardware net-gain claim precedes the first-of-a-kind machine. See what we will not claim and the open-science flywheel.

title: Frozen-Design Discipline
lede: We attach every claim to a specific, versioned design, so environmental statements refer to a real configuration, not a moving target.
body: An environmental claim is meaningless if the design it describes keeps changing. Kronos practices frozen-design discipline: key configurations are fixed and versioned, and claims attach to a specific frozen design. When we cite the breeder's fusion power of 88.7 MW or the burner's 26.49 T plug, those numbers belong to a defined configuration, not a shifting sketch.
Every performance and footprint claim references a specific configuration
Changes are versioned, so old claims can be traced to old designs
Comparisons are fair because both sides name their configuration
Reproducibility is possible because the subject of analysis is fixed

The frozen canon includes the breeder's Q_sci of 3.424, plasma current of 9.86 MA, peak field of 16.84 T, and negative triangularity of -0.30, together with the burner's parameters. Freezing these lets outside reviewers check our work against a stable target — a precondition for the reproducibility that underlies environmental trust.

<svg viewBox='0 0 420 120' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Versioned frozen designs'><g font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='11' fill='#232C39' text-anchor='middle'><rect x='40' y='40' width='90' height='45' rx='6' fill='none' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='85' y='67'>v1 frozen</text><rect x='165' y='40' width='90' height='45' rx='6' fill='none' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='210' y='67'>v2 frozen</text><rect x='290' y='40' width='90' height='45' rx='6' fill='#D4AD5C' opacity='0.4' stroke='#D4AD5C' stroke-width='2'/><text x='335' y='67'>current</text></g><line x1='130' y1='62' x2='165' y2='62' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='1'/><line x1='255' y1='62' x2='290' y2='62' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='1'/></svg>

Freezing does not mean refusing to improve; it means improving in versioned steps rather than in an untracked drift. Each frozen configuration is a checkpoint against which claims, footprints, and predictions can be pinned. When the design advances, the old claims remain traceable to the old design, so the record never quietly rewrites itself.
See reproducibility as environmental trust and designing digitally before building.

title: Designing Digitally Before Building
lede: Simulating exhaustively before cutting metal saves materials, energy, and risk — an environmental practice as much as an engineering one.
body: Iterate in software, not in steel

Every physical prototype consumes materials and energy and, if it fails, produces waste. Every simulation consumes only computation. Kronos designs and tests digitally before building, iterating in software where iteration is fast and reversible. This is standard good engineering, but it is also an environmental practice: fewer wasted physical builds.
Model plasma physics and machine behavior in simulation
Explore design levers digitally, such as the breeder's tritium breeding ratio range
Catch failure modes before they are built into metal
Freeze a design only when the digital case is strong

Both machines are, today, design and simulation studies. Breeder construction begins Q2 2027; before then, the work is digital. This ordering means the physical resources committed to construction go toward a design already stress-tested in software, not toward a first guess.

<svg viewBox='0 0 420 120' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Simulate many, build one'><g fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='10' text-anchor='middle'><circle cx='60' cy='40' r='10' fill='none' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='1.5'/><circle cx='60' cy='70' r='10' fill='none' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='1.5'/><circle cx='60' cy='100' r='10' fill='none' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='60' y='18'>simulate many</text><line x1='75' y1='70' x2='200' y2='70' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='1.5'/><rect x='200' y='55' width='40' height='30' rx='4' fill='#D4AD5C'/><text x='300' y='73'>build the proven one</text></g></svg>

The environmental savings compound with the engineering ones. A failed physical prototype is not only lost time; it is embodied material and energy converted into scrap. Exhausting the reversible failures in simulation means the material failures happen far less often. Good sequencing is itself a form of resource stewardship.
This underpins our digital-twin work and connects to the precautionary approach and frozen-design discipline.

title: The EHS Connection
lede: Environment, health, and safety are one discipline; our planetary mission and our EHS practice share the same evidence and standards.
body: Environment, health, and safety (EHS) are often treated as separate compliance boxes. In practice they are one discipline: protecting people and ecosystems from the hazards of an energy technology. Our planetary mission and our EHS practice draw on the same evidence, the same conservative design margins, and the same honesty about risk.
Where environment meets health and safety
Radiological safety governs tritium handling and neutron shielding
Materials choices affect both worker safety and end-of-life environmental burden
Water and effluent management protect ecosystems and communities alike
Honest hazard disclosure serves both regulators and the public

The breeder's 14 MeV neutrons and tritium inventory, and the burner's lower but nonzero neutron fraction of 5.44%, are the central EHS considerations. We treat them as design inputs from the start, not as problems to manage after the fact — see radiological honesty and activation and materials choices.

<svg viewBox='0 0 260 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Environment health safety overlap'><circle cx='100' cy='80' r='55' fill='#232C39' opacity='0.18'/><circle cx='160' cy='80' r='55' fill='#232C39' opacity='0.18'/><circle cx='130' cy='130' r='55' fill='#D4AD5C' opacity='0.25'/><g font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='12' fill='#232C39' text-anchor='middle'><text x='75' y='60'>Env</text><text x='185' y='60'>Health</text><text x='130' y='160'>Safety</text></g></svg>

Treating these as one discipline has a practical payoff: a decision made for safety, such as robust neutron shielding, often improves environmental outcomes too, and vice versa. Separating them into unrelated compliance exercises tends to miss those shared gains and to let each domain assume the others are someone else's problem.
This is why stewardship at Kronos is inseparable from safety — see stewardship as an engineering discipline.

title: Radiological Honesty
lede: Fusion involves radioactive materials; we describe tritium and neutron hazards plainly and design to contain and minimize them.
body: Fusion is often described as clean, and in important ways it is. But it is not free of radiological hazard, and pretending otherwise would betray the honesty this mission is built on. The breeder (Hyperion) handles tritium, which is radioactive, and produces 14 MeV neutrons that activate structures. These are real hazards that responsible design contains and minimizes.
What the hazards are, and are not
Tritium: radioactive, mobile, short half-life; requires careful containment
Neutron activation: makes structures radioactive over time; material-dependent
Not present: the long-lived high-level spent-fuel waste of fission
Not present: any runaway chain reaction; fusion stops when conditions are not maintained

The burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) has a far smaller neutron burden, with only 5.44% of its energy as neutrons, which reduces activation relative to a D-T machine. But smaller is not zero, and we say so. Honest radiological communication states both the reduction and the residual.

<svg viewBox='0 0 420 120' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Containment layers'><circle cx='120' cy='60' r='12' fill='#D4AD5C'/><circle cx='120' cy='60' r='26' fill='none' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='1.5'/><circle cx='120' cy='60' r='40' fill='none' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='250' y='50' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='11'>source</text><text x='250' y='72' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='11'>shielding</text><text x='250' y='94' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='11'>containment</text></svg>

The honest framing is comparative and specific rather than reassuring in the abstract. Fusion's radiological profile differs from fission's in kind, not merely degree: no spent-fuel waste stream, no chain reaction to arrest, but real tritium and activation hazards that demand serious containment. Stating exactly which risks apply, and which do not, is what earns the word clean.
Containment and material selection are the levers; see activation and materials choices and fusion waste, stated honestly.

title: Activation and Materials Choices
lede: Neutrons make structures radioactive; choosing low-activation materials shortens how long that material stays hazardous.
body: When neutrons strike a material, they can transmute its atoms into radioactive isotopes — a process called activation. For the breeder (Hyperion), with its 14 MeV neutron flux, activation of the surrounding structure is the principal source of radioactive waste. How bad and how long-lived that waste is depends heavily on which materials are used.

Some materials activate into short-lived isotopes that decay to safe levels relatively quickly; others produce long-lived isotopes that remain hazardous for far longer. Choosing low-activation materials is therefore one of the most consequential environmental decisions in the design, and we treat it as such rather than defaulting to whatever is easiest to fabricate.
Prefer materials that activate into shorter-lived isotopes
Weigh activation against structural and thermal performance
Account for end-of-life handling from the start
Reduce total activated mass through compact design

The burner's low neutron fraction of 5.44% means much less activation to begin with, which is a structural advantage of the D-3He reaction — though it depends on scarce helium-3, as noted in helium-3 and the planet.

<svg viewBox='0 0 420 120' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Decay of activated material over time'><line x1='30' y1='95' x2='400' y2='95' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='1.5'/><line x1='30' y1='20' x2='30' y2='95' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M30 30 C120 90 220 92 400 93' fill='none' stroke='#D4AD5C' stroke-width='2.5'/><text x='210' y='115' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='10' text-anchor='middle'>time → hazard falls with good material choice</text></svg>

Because activation depends on both flux and material, the same neutron environment can leave one component safe within decades and another hazardous for far longer. Treating material selection as an environmental decision, weighed alongside strength and cost of fabrication, is how the eventual waste burden is minimized before a single neutron is ever produced.
This decision propagates into decommissioning thinking and links to materials and the Earth.

title: Decommissioning Thinking
lede: A plant's end of life is a design input, not an afterthought; we plan for retirement while the machine is still on paper.
body: Designing for the end at the beginning

Many industrial legacies are burdens precisely because no one planned for their end. Kronos treats decommissioning as a design input from the start. How components will be removed, how activated material will be handled, and how much can be recycled are questions we ask while the machine is still a design, not after it has operated for decades.
What good end-of-life design looks like
Modular components that can be removed and replaced without demolishing the whole
Low-activation materials so retired structures reach safe levels sooner
Maximized recyclability to return material to supply chains
Clear records of what was exposed to neutrons and for how long

Because the breeder produces activated structural material, decommissioning is where its main waste stream is finally handled. Planning for that stream in advance — including the material choices in activation and materials choices — is how a machine avoids becoming a legacy problem.

<svg viewBox='0 0 420 120' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Modular removal and recycling'><rect x='40' y='40' width='40' height='50' fill='#232C39'/><rect x='85' y='40' width='40' height='50' fill='#232C39' opacity='0.6'/><rect x='130' y='40' width='40' height='50' fill='#232C39' opacity='0.3'/><line x1='185' y1='65' x2='250' y2='65' stroke='#D4AD5C' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='320' cy='65' r='30' fill='none' stroke='#D4AD5C' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M320 40 A25 25 0 0 1 344 68' fill='none' stroke='#D4AD5C' stroke-width='2'/><text x='320' y='70' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='9' text-anchor='middle'>recycle</text></svg>

The contrast we want to avoid is the industrial site left as a burden because its end was never designed. By making removal, sorting, and recycling explicit design requirements now, the eventual retirement becomes a planned operation rather than an inherited problem. A machine designed for its own end is a smaller legacy than one that was not.
End-of-life planning is part of lifecycle thinking and from extraction to stewardship.

title: The Long-Now Perspective
lede: Energy decisions echo for generations; we try to act as good ancestors, weighing consequences on the timescale of the biosphere.
body: The infrastructure we build now shapes emissions, land, and materials for generations. A long-now perspective asks whether a decision will look wise not next quarter but in fifty or a hundred years — the timescale on which climate and ecosystems actually respond. This is the clock the biosphere keeps.
Preferring fuels abundant enough to last centuries, not decades
Designing for end of life so we do not bequeath cleanup burdens
Choosing reversible, testable steps over irreversible bets
Publishing openly so future teams inherit knowledge, not just hardware

Our staged, cautious timeline reflects this: build a first-of-a-kind, prove it, then scale. We do not rush to fleets before the physics is demonstrated, because a mistake made at scale echoes far longer than the time saved by hurrying. The breeder's construction start in Q2 2027 and first-tritium target around 2030 are steps on a much longer road.

<svg viewBox='0 0 440 100' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Long timeline of consequences'><line x1='20' y1='55' x2='420' y2='55' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='60' cy='55' r='5' fill='#D4AD5C'/><text x='60' y='80' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='10' text-anchor='middle'>now</text><circle cx='240' cy='55' r='4' fill='#232C39'/><text x='240' y='80' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='10' text-anchor='middle'>decades</text><circle cx='400' cy='55' r='4' fill='#232C39'/><text x='400' y='80' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='10' text-anchor='middle'>generations</text></svg>

Acting as a good ancestor is a demanding standard because the people it serves cannot speak for themselves today. It argues for reversible steps, honest records, and fuels abundant enough to last, so that a future generation inherits capability and knowledge rather than cleanup and depletion. The long clock is unforgiving of shortcuts taken to save a little time now.
This connects to the healed-Earth aspiration and building to uplift humanity.

title: The Planetary-Boundaries Framing
lede: The biosphere has limits humanity should stay within; clean firm energy touches several of those boundaries at once.
body: The planetary-boundaries framing describes environmental limits — for climate, land use, freshwater, biogeochemical flows, and more — within which humanity can operate safely. Crossing them risks destabilizing the systems life depends on. Energy is entangled with several of these boundaries simultaneously, which is why the energy choice matters so broadly.
Climate change: driven largely by combustion emissions
Land-system change: extraction and siting occupy and disturb land
Freshwater use: thermal generation draws on water
Biogeochemical flows: pollution from combustion alters nitrogen and other cycles

A clean firm source can ease pressure on the climate boundary directly and on the pollution boundaries by ending combustion. It does not by itself resolve land, water, or material boundaries — those depend on how the technology is built and sited, which we treat honestly on their own pages. No energy technology sits comfortably inside every boundary.

<svg viewBox='0 0 240 240' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Boundaries as concentric safe operating space'><circle cx='120' cy='120' r='90' fill='none' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='1.5' stroke-dasharray='4 4'/><circle cx='120' cy='120' r='55' fill='#D4AD5C' opacity='0.2' stroke='#D4AD5C' stroke-width='2'/><text x='120' y='118' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='11' text-anchor='middle'>safe operating</text><text x='120' y='134' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='11' text-anchor='middle'>space</text><text x='120' y='30' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='9' text-anchor='middle'>boundary</text></svg>

No single technology, including ours, sits comfortably within every boundary at once; each involves trade-offs among them. The value of the framing is that it forces those trade-offs into view rather than letting a benefit on one boundary hide a cost on another. We use it to keep our own accounting honest across more than just the climate axis.
See energy and the biosphere and the biosphere and thermal limits.

title: Energy Return and Society
lede: A source worth building must return far more usable energy than it takes to build and run it; that surplus is what powers civilization.
body: An energy source is only useful if it returns substantially more energy over its life than was invested to build, fuel, and run it. That surplus is what runs hospitals, farms, and cities beyond the energy sector itself. A source that barely breaks even, no matter how clean, cannot carry a civilization.
Why we are candid about this

For fusion, the honest statement is that net energy return is exactly what remains to be demonstrated in hardware. The breeder's scientific gain figure, Q_sci of 3.424, is a plasma-physics result from design study, not a whole-plant energy return, and not yet a hardware measurement. We make no hardware net-gain claim before the first-of-a-kind machine operates around 2030.
Surplus energy is what makes a source worth building
Plasma gain is not the same as whole-plant net energy return
We claim no hardware net gain before first-of-a-kind operation

<svg viewBox='0 0 420 120' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Energy invested versus returned'><rect x='60' y='60' width='40' height='30' fill='#232C39'/><text x='80' y='108' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='10' text-anchor='middle'>invested</text><rect x='200' y='30' width='40' height='60' fill='#D4AD5C'/><text x='220' y='108' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='10' text-anchor='middle'>returned</text><text x='150' y='55' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='14'>→</text><text x='300' y='60' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='10'>surplus powers society</text></svg>

The distinction between plasma gain and whole-plant return is one we insist on because it is so often blurred. A machine can reach an impressive plasma-physics result and still not deliver net usable energy once the whole plant is accounted for. Which is why our gain figure is presented as what it is — a design-study physics result, not a demonstrated societal surplus.
This candor is central to what we will not claim and to the energy-poverty problem, which needs real surplus to solve.

title: Grid Resilience and Climate Adaptation
lede: A warming world brings harsher weather to the grid; firm, sited generation can make power systems more resilient, not just cleaner.
body: Climate action is usually framed as mitigation — cutting emissions. But a changing climate also stresses the systems we already depend on, including the electricity grid, through heat waves, storms, and shifting demand. Adaptation matters alongside mitigation. Firm, sited clean generation can serve both: it cuts emissions and it hardens the grid.
Weather-independent output when storms cut variable generation
On-site or near-load generation reduces exposure to long transmission lines
Continuous supply for critical loads during extreme events
Diversity of sources makes the whole system harder to knock out

The burner housings are studied for exactly such sited, critical loads: MetroVolt for continuous compute and Aegis for fixed installations. Reducing dependence on long, storm-exposed transmission is a resilience benefit distinct from the emissions benefit.

<svg viewBox='0 0 420 130' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Sited generation resilient to storm'><path d='M60 30 q20 15 0 30 q-20 15 0 30' fill='none' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='1.5'/><rect x='150' y='55' width='70' height='40' rx='6' fill='#D4AD5C'/><text x='185' y='80' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='10' text-anchor='middle'>firm site</text><rect x='260' y='55' width='90' height='40' fill='none' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='305' y='80' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='10' text-anchor='middle'>critical load</text><line x1='220' y1='75' x2='260' y2='75' stroke='#D4AD5C' stroke-width='3'/></svg>

Resilience and cleanliness usually get argued separately, as if adaptation and mitigation competed for attention. Firm, sited clean generation collapses that trade-off: the same asset that lowers emissions also keeps critical load served when a storm takes down the lines. Designing for both at once is more honest about the world these machines would actually operate in.

We claim no operating resilience record, because the machines are unbuilt. The point is design intent: firm, sited clean power addresses adaptation and mitigation together. See why firm power matters.

title: The Moral Case for Clean Energy
lede: Pollution and climate harm fall hardest on those least responsible; clean, abundant energy is a question of justice as well as ecology.
body: The costs of dirty energy — polluted air, climate disruption, degraded land — fall most heavily on communities that contributed least to causing them and can least afford to escape them. A clean-energy mission that ignores this distribution addresses ecology while sidestepping justice. We do not separate the two.
Stop imposing pollution on those who did not choose it
Extend enough clean energy to those who currently have too little

This is why we reject a framing of environmentalism as pure restraint. Restraint asked only of those with little is not justice. The moral case is for abundant clean energy widely shared, so that health and opportunity do not require burning fuel that harms someone downwind. See the energy-poverty problem.

<svg viewBox='0 0 420 120' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Balancing harm and access'><line x1='210' y1='30' x2='210' y2='95' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='120' y1='55' x2='300' y2='55' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='120' cy='55' r='6' fill='#232C39'/><circle cx='300' cy='55' r='6' fill='#D4AD5C'/><text x='120' y='85' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='10' text-anchor='middle'>less harm</text><text x='300' y='85' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='10' text-anchor='middle'>more access</text></svg>

We are careful not to launder a business into a moral crusade. The obligation described here is a reason to build well and share widely, not a certificate that we already have. The machines are unbuilt and the justice they might serve is prospective. What the moral case does is set the standard against which we expect to be judged if we succeed.

We hold this as a value that shapes what we build toward, not a benefit we have delivered. The machines are unbuilt. The obligation is to build them, if we can, in service of that justice — see building to uplift humanity.

title: Humility About What We Don't Know
lede: Fusion is hard and unfinished; stating our uncertainties plainly is part of being trustworthy about the planet.
body: Fusion energy is one of the hardest engineering problems attempted, and it is not finished. Kronos has not built a working power plant. Treating our designs as if their benefits were already realized would be dishonest, and dishonesty is corrosive to the environmental trust this mission depends on. So we state our uncertainties plainly.
What we do not yet know
Whether the machines will achieve hardware net energy gain
How real components will behave over years of neutron exposure
How a helium-3 supply for a burner fleet would be secured at scale
How every lifecycle footprint estimate compares to eventual measured data

Naming these is not weakness; it is the precondition for being believed when we do report a solid result. Our staged timeline, pre-registered predictions, and open data all exist so that our uncertainties are visible and our confirmed claims are trustworthy. See pre-registered predictions and what we will not claim.

<svg viewBox='0 0 420 110' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Known and unknown regions'><rect x='40' y='35' width='140' height='45' rx='6' fill='#D4AD5C' opacity='0.4' stroke='#D4AD5C' stroke-width='2'/><text x='110' y='62' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='11' text-anchor='middle'>what we know</text><rect x='230' y='35' width='150' height='45' rx='6' fill='none' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='1.5' stroke-dasharray='5 4'/><text x='305' y='62' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='11' text-anchor='middle'>what we don't</text></svg>

Stated uncertainties are also a defense against our own enthusiasm. It is easy, working on something you believe in, to let hope harden into assertion. Writing down what remains unknown, and returning to that list as results arrive, is a structural check on that drift — one that keeps the confident claims rare enough to be worth something.
Humility also keeps us open to being wrong — the heart of the precautionary approach.

title: Fusion Among Clean Technologies
lede: We reject either-or thinking; fusion should earn a place in a broad clean-energy portfolio, not displace the technologies already working.
body: Not a silver bullet, a portfolio member

Some technology stories cast a favored option as the one true answer that makes all others obsolete. That framing is both wrong and harmful. The clean-energy transition needs solar, wind, storage, geothermal, advanced fission, efficiency, and grid improvements — all of them, deployed now. Fusion, if it works, joins that portfolio; it does not replace it.
Solar and wind: abundant energy where conditions allow
Geothermal and fission: firm clean power today
Fusion: a candidate firm source, still to be proven

Casting fusion as a reason to slow deployment of proven renewables would be a real environmental harm, because the atmosphere responds to emissions cut now, not to promises of a better source later. We are explicit: build what works today, and develop fusion as an addition, not an excuse.

<svg viewBox='0 0 420 120' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Portfolio of clean sources'><g font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='9' fill='#232C39' text-anchor='middle'><rect x='30' y='45' width='60' height='40' fill='#232C39' opacity='0.7'/><text x='60' y='100'>solar</text><rect x='100' y='45' width='60' height='40' fill='#232C39' opacity='0.55'/><text x='130' y='100'>wind</text><rect x='170' y='45' width='60' height='40' fill='#232C39' opacity='0.4'/><text x='200' y='100'>storage</text><rect x='240' y='45' width='60' height='40' fill='#232C39' opacity='0.3'/><text x='270' y='100'>geo/fission</text><rect x='310' y='45' width='60' height='40' fill='#D4AD5C'/><text x='340' y='100'>fusion</text></g></svg>

The strongest version of our position is that we would rather be one useful member of a diverse clean portfolio than the imagined hero of a story that slows real deployment. Emissions respond to what is built now. Any framing of fusion that discourages proven technologies today would do environmental harm even if the fusion eventually worked.
This is the humility of firm versus intermittent extended to the whole field, and it is why we practice open science that lifts everyone.

title: The Biosphere and Thermal Limits
lede: All energy use ends as heat; naming this ultimate limit keeps our ambitions honest even for a carbon-free source.
body: Even a perfectly carbon-free energy source is not free of physical limits. By thermodynamics, essentially all energy humanity uses eventually degrades into waste heat delivered to the environment. Today this is a negligible effect beside greenhouse warming, but it is a real ceiling on how much energy a planet's surface can absorb without warming from the heat itself.

Naming this limit is a matter of intellectual honesty. It means that abundant clean energy is not a license for unbounded growth in energy use forever; it shifts the binding constraint from emissions to heat rejection at some far-off scale. Acknowledging that keeps the healed-Earth aspiration grounded rather than utopian.
Carbon-free removes the greenhouse constraint, not the heat constraint
Waste heat is negligible today, but not infinitely so
Abundance still asks for wisdom about how much we use

<svg viewBox='0 0 420 130' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Energy in becomes heat out'><circle cx='120' cy='65' r='40' fill='none' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='2'/><text x='120' y='69' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='10' text-anchor='middle'>energy use</text><path d='M162 65 h60' stroke='#D4AD5C' stroke-width='2' marker-end='url(#h)'/><defs><marker id='h' markerWidth='8' markerHeight='8' refX='4' refY='4' orient='auto'><path d='M0 0 L8 4 L0 8 z' fill='#D4AD5C'/></marker></defs><text x='300' y='69' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='10' text-anchor='middle'>waste heat</text></svg>

Naming the heat limit is not fatalism; today it is far from binding and greenhouse warming dominates entirely. But acknowledging it keeps the aspiration of abundance from sliding into a fantasy of infinite growth. Even the cleanest energy asks for judgment about how much a civilization needs, not merely how cleanly it can be produced.
This is the far horizon of the planetary-boundaries framing and a reason for the restraint in the long-now perspective.

title: From Extraction to Stewardship
lede: Abundant clean energy could let a civilization recycle rather than perpetually mine — shifting its relationship to the Earth.
body: Industrial civilization has largely run on extraction: dig up material and fuel, use them once, discard the remains. This works only while the crust and the atmosphere seem infinite. They are not. A different relationship — stewardship — treats materials as loops to be closed and the biosphere as something to maintain, not deplete.

Recycling is often more energy-intensive than mining; that is a large part of why we mine instead. Abundant clean energy changes that calculation. When energy is clean and plentiful, closing material loops stops carrying an emissions penalty, and stewardship becomes practical rather than merely virtuous. Energy is the hinge on which extraction can turn into stewardship.
Recycling trades material extraction for energy input
Clean abundant energy removes the emissions penalty of that trade
Fusion fuels are abundant, reinforcing the shift away from scarce extraction

<svg viewBox='0 0 420 130' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Linear extraction versus circular stewardship'><line x1='30' y1='40' x2='180' y2='40' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='2' marker-end='url(#l)'/><defs><marker id='l' markerWidth='8' markerHeight='8' refX='4' refY='4' orient='auto'><path d='M0 0 L8 4 L0 8 z' fill='#232C39'/></marker></defs><text x='100' y='30' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='9' text-anchor='middle'>extract → discard</text><circle cx='320' cy='60' r='38' fill='none' stroke='#D4AD5C' stroke-width='2.5'/><path d='M320 22 A38 38 0 0 1 355 55' fill='none' stroke='#D4AD5C' stroke-width='2.5' marker-end='url(#l)'/><text x='320' y='64' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='9' text-anchor='middle'>reuse</text></svg>

None of this happens automatically. Abundant clean energy makes stewardship possible, not inevitable; the loops still have to be designed and the incentives still have to favor closing them. But removing the emissions penalty on recycling is a genuine unlock, because it turns a choice that currently costs the atmosphere into one that no longer does.
We design our own machines with this in mind — see decommissioning thinking and materials and the Earth.

title: Building to Uplift Humanity
lede: The purpose behind the physics: energy that raises human dignity and gives the living world room to recover.
body: The physics is demanding and the timeline is long, so the purpose has to be clear. Kronos exists to help provide energy that raises human dignity — health, education, opportunity, and clean air — while giving the biosphere room to recover. That is what we mean by building to uplift humanity. It is the reason the hard work is worth doing.
Air free of combustion products for the communities near power
Enough reliable energy for clinics, schools, and industry
Medical isotopes from the breeder's neutrons for human health
A material economy that recycles instead of endlessly extracting

We are careful to hold this as motivation, not as an accomplishment. The machines are design and simulation studies; they have uplifted no one yet. The honest claim is about intent and direction, backed by the discipline — open data, pre-registered predictions, staged testing — that would make the intent real if the physics closes.

<svg viewBox='0 0 420 120' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Energy lifting human wellbeing'><line x1='30' y1='95' x2='400' y2='95' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M40 90 L140 70 L240 50 L360 30' fill='none' stroke='#D4AD5C' stroke-width='2.5'/><g fill='#232C39'><circle cx='40' cy='90' r='4'/><circle cx='140' cy='70' r='4'/><circle cx='240' cy='50' r='4'/><circle cx='360' cy='30' r='4'/></g><text x='210' y='115' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='10' text-anchor='middle'>clean energy → human wellbeing</text></svg>

We separate motivation from accomplishment on purpose, because conflating them is how mission language turns into marketing. The uplift described here is a direction of travel and a test we invite others to hold us to, backed by open data and staged proof. If the physics does not close, the honest response is to say so, not to redescribe the aspiration as a result.
This purpose sits above every technical page — see the healed-Earth aspiration and the moral case for clean energy.

title: What We Will Not Claim
lede: Honesty is defined as much by restraint as by assertion; here are the environmental claims we deliberately refuse to make.
body: Environmental communication is full of claims that outrun the evidence. On this mission, honesty means naming what we will not say as clearly as what we will. These refusals are not hedging; they are the boundary that makes our positive claims worth trusting.
That either machine has achieved hardware net energy gain — it has not; we make no such claim before the first-of-a-kind operates
That fusion is entirely waste-free — the breeder produces activated structural material
That a burner fleet's helium-3 supply is solved — it is not
That our footprint figures are measured plant data — they are design-study estimates
That fusion should displace renewables — it should complement them

We also refuse to attach economics of any kind to environmental claims, and to present a single design number as if the design were settled when it is a studied range — as with the breeder's tritium breeding ratio across 1.1, 1.5, and 1.8.

<svg viewBox='0 0 420 110' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Line between claimed and not claimed'><line x1='210' y1='20' x2='210' y2='90' stroke='#232C39' stroke-width='2' stroke-dasharray='5 4'/><text x='110' y='58' fill='#232C39' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='11' text-anchor='middle'>what we claim</text><text x='315' y='58' fill='#D4AD5C' font-family='Georgia,serif' font-size='11' text-anchor='middle'>what we won't</text></svg>

Keeping this list explicit and public is itself a commitment. It gives readers a fixed standard to hold us to and makes backsliding visible: if a future claim of ours crosses one of these lines, the crossing is on the record. Refusals stated in advance are harder to quietly abandon than good intentions kept only in mind.
This page is the backstop for every other environmental claim on the site. See humility about what we don't know and honest environmental accounting.

title: The Mission, in One Page
lede: Clean firm energy, developed in the open with honest limits, in service of people and the biosphere — the whole argument, briefly.
body: Energy sits upstream of nearly every pressure on the biosphere. A clean, firm, non-combustion source could relieve several of those pressures at once — climate, air, and, if it enables recycling, materials. Fusion is a candidate for that firm role. We are studying two machines toward it, and we are honest that they are not yet built.
Breeder (Hyperion): a D-T spherical tokamak, tritium and helium-3 and 14 MeV neutrons; construction begins Q2 2027, first tritium targeted around 2030
Burner (Aegis / MetroVolt): a D-3He tandem-mirror generator with direct energy conversion and a low neutron fraction of 5.44%, for fixed installations and data centers

We make no hardware net-gain claim before the first-of-a-kind machine operates. Where the science is unsettled — the tritium breeding ratio, the helium-3 supply — we say so. Every environmental figure we give is a design-study estimate, labeled as such.

In the open. We publish papers with DOIs, share data under open licenses, pre-register falsifiable predictions, keep a reproducible analysis record, freeze designs so claims attach to real configurations, and design digitally before cutting metal. These practices are how environmental trust is earned rather than asserted.
